title: Chapter XVII

teacherSummary.text: The creature demands a female companion as wretched as himself, promising to withdraw to South America. Moved and afraid, Victor agrees.

vocabulary.definition: Incapable of being passed over, surmounted, or overcome
vocabulary.context: But that cannot be; the human senses are insurmountable barriers to our union.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “insurmountable”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: This you alone can do; and I demand it of you as a right which you must not refuse to concede.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “concede”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + ced (Latin cedere, "to go, yield"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A thing of very little value or importance
vocabulary.context: I must not be trifled with: and I demand an answer.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “trifle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: One who, or that which, defends or shields from injury, evil, oppression, etc.; a defender
vocabulary.context: I thought of the promise of virtues which he had displayed on the opening of his existence, and the subsequent blight of all kindly feeling by the loathing and scorn which his protectors had manifested towards him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “protector”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + -or (Latin -or, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I compassionated him, and sometimes felt a wish to console him; but when I looked upon him, when I saw the filthy mass that moved and talked, my heart sickened, and my feelings were altered to those of horror and hatred.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sicken”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To put each in the place of the other
vocabulary.context: “You must create a female for me, with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “interchange”: inter- (Latin inter, "between"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: His power and threats were not omitted in my calculations: a creature who could exist in the ice-caves of the glaciers, and hide himself from pursuit among the ridges of inaccessible precipices, was a being possessing faculties it would be vain to cope with.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “precipice”: pre- (Latin prae, "before"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To tell, rehearse, or recite, as a story
vocabulary.context: The latter part of his tale had kindled anew in me the anger that had died away while he narrated his peaceful life among the cottagers, and, as he said this, I could no longer suppress the rage that burned within me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “narrate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: (Fort.) A carpentry obstruction, stockade, or other obstacle made in a passage in order to stop an enemy
vocabulary.context: But that cannot be; the human senses are insurmountable barriers to our union.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “barrier”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To persist in any business or enterprise undertaken
vocabulary.context: How can you, who long for the love and sympathy of man, persevere in this exile?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “persevere”: per- (Latin per, "through, thoroughly"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Debates on whether humans have natural rights to companionship and happiness echo Enlightenment philosophy.

significance: This bargain is the hinge of the plot; Victor's later choice will decide everyone's fate.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XVII,” how does Shelley show the demand for a companion? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the theme you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XVII develops the idea of the demand for a companion. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of theme and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses theme in Chapter XVII to complicate the reader's understanding of the demand for a companion. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XVII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the demand for a companion responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XVII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the demand for a companion. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

annotationFocus.passage: “You must create a female for me, with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being. This you alone can do; and I demand it of you as a right which you must not refuse to concede.”

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Is the creature's request fair? What risks does Victor consider? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are insurmountable, concede, trifled, protectors, sickened. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “But that cannot be; the human senses are insurmountable barriers to our union.” Webster's says: Incapable of being passed over, surmounted, or overcome. Now the word history: “insurmountable”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “concede”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + ced (Latin cedere, "to go, yield"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “trifle”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Debates on whether humans have natural rights to companionship and happiness echo Enlightenment philosophy. Why does this chapter matter? This bargain is the hinge of the plot; Victor's later choice will decide everyone's fate. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for theme.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see theme, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the demand for a companion.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Theme, Characterization, Conflict.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of theme. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “You must create a female for me, with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being. This you alone can do; and I demand it of you as a right which you must not refuse to concede.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Theme, Characterization, Conflict: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XVII,” how does Shelley show the demand for a companion? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the theme you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the demand for a companion, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how theme shapes the demand for a companion. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
